summary:
Penza Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and Russian government warnings address LGBT travellers directly.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the framework applying here: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the propaganda law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The same note records that at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, and that 81 people across 98 court cases since January 2024 had been convicted of administrative offences for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation enabled criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison and built on the 2013 propaganda law. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity: Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Propaganda-law cases have grown eighteenfold over a decade, and the fines attached to them have generated more than 60 million rubles for the state budget in two years, indicating routine rather than exceptional application of the statutes.

The post-designation response was immediate: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, police raided LGBTQ-friendly venues in Moscow, searching and photographing about 100 patrons at one bar and hitting at least two others the same night. Detainees have died in state custody, most recently a man held on extremism charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency, found dead in a pretrial detention facility in December 2024.

Foreign governments treat the risk as acute. The US State Department places Russia at its highest advisory level with explicit warnings for LGBT travellers, while the UK Home Office recognises LGBT+ Russians as a particular social group for refugee purposes, and Human Rights Watch has asked governments to offer safe haven to those leaving the country.

Coercive practices against transgender people sit alongside formal legal penalties. A documented case saw a transgender woman confined for nine months in a conversion-therapy facility and forced to take testosterone, showing that risk to trans visitors and residents is not confined to court proceedings.
